source_text: Ἐπεὶ δ᾿ ἅπαξ εἰς τὸν περὶ τῶν προφητῶν ἤλθομεν λόγον, Ἰουδαίοις μὲν, τοῖς πιστεύουσι θείῳ πνεύματι αὐτοὺς λελαληκέναι, οὐ μόνον οὐκ ἔσται ἀχρήσιμα τὰ ἐποισθησόμενα (ἀλλὰ) καὶ τοῖς εὐγνωμονοῦσι δὲ τῶν Ἑλλήνων. πρὸς οὓς ἐροῦμεν ὅτι ἀναγκαῖον παραδέξασθαι ὅτι καὶ Ἰουδαῖοι προφήτας εἶχον, εἴπερ ἔμελλον συνέχεσθαι ἐν τῇ δοθείσῃ αὐτοῖς νομοθεσίᾳ καὶ πιστεύειν τῷ δημιουργῷ, καθάπερ εἰλήφεισαν, καὶ ὅσον ἐπὶ τῷ νόμῳ μὴ ἔχειν ἀφορμὰς ἀποστῆναι εἰς τὴν τῶν ἐθνῶν πολυθεότητα. τὸ δ᾿ ἀναγκαῖον οὕτω παραστήσομεν. „τὰ ἔθνη,“ ὡς γέγραπται καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ τῶν Ἰουδαίων νόμῳ, „κληδόνων καὶ μαντειῶν ἀκούσονται“· τῷ δὲ λαῷ ἐκείνῳ εἴρηται· „σοὶ δὲ οὐχ οὕτως ἔδωκε κύριος ὁ θεός σου.“ καὶ ἐπιφέρεται τούτῳ τὸ „προφήτην ἐκ τῶν ἀδελφῶν σου ἀναστήσει σοι κύριος ὁ θεός σου.“ εἴπερ οὖν τῶν ἐθνῶν χρωμένων μαντείαις εἴτε διὰ „κληδόνων“ εἴτε δι᾿ οἰωνῶν εἴτε δι᾿ ὀρνίθων εἴτε δι᾿ ἐγγαστριμύθων εἴτε καὶ διὰ τῶν τὴν θυτικὴν ἐπαγγελλομένων εἴτε καὶ διὰ Χαλδαίων γενεθλιαλογούντων, ἅπερ πάντα Ἰουδαίοις ἀπείρητο. Ἰουδαῖοι εἰ μηδεμίαν εἶχον παραμυθίαν γνώσεως τῶν μελλόντων, ὑπ᾿ αὐτῆς ἂν τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης περὶ τὴν γνῶσιν λιχνείας τῶν ἐσομένων ἀγόμενοι κατεφρόνησαν μὲν ἂν τῶν ἰδίων ὡς οὐδὲν ἐχόντων θεῖον ἐν ἑαυτοῖς καὶ οὐκ ἂν μετὰ Μω(??)σέα προφήτην προσήκαντο οὐδ᾿ ἀνέγραψαν αὐτῶν τοὺς λόγους, αὐτόμολοι δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν μαντεῖα καὶ χρηστήρια μετέστησαν ἢ ἐπεχείρησαν ἂν ἱδρῦσαί τι τοιοῦτον καὶ παρ᾿ ἑαυτοῖς. ὥστ᾿ οὐδὲν ἄτοπόν ἐστι καὶ περὶ τῶν τυχόντων τοὺς παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς προφήτας εἰς παραμυθίαν τῶν τὰ τοιαῦτα ποθούντων προειρηκέναι, ὥστε καὶ „περὶ ὄνων ἀπολωλυιῶν“ προφητεύειν τὸν Σαμουὴλ καὶ περὶ νόσου παιδὸς βασιλικοῦ τὸν ἐν τῇ τρίτῃ τῶν Βασιλειῶν ἀναγεγραμμένον. πῶς δ᾿ ἂν τῷ βουλομένῳ ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων μαντείαν λαβεῖν ἐπέπλησσον οἱ τὰ τοῦ νόμου Ἰουδαίων πρεσβεύοντες; ὥσπερ εὑρίσκεται Ἠλίας τῷ Ὀχοζίᾳ ἐπιπλήσσων καὶ λέγων· „εἰ παρὰ τὸ μὴ εἶναι θεὸν ἐν Ἰσραὴλ ὑμεῖς πορεύεσθε ἐκζητῆσαι ἐν τῇ Βαὰλ μυῖαν θεὸν Ἀκκαρῶν.“
pass_a_gloss: Since we have once come to the discourse about the prophets, for the Jews, who believe that they spoke by the divine Spirit, the things that will be said will not be useless, but also for the Greeks who are grateful. To whom we will say that it is necessary to accept that the Jews also had prophets, if indeed they were going to be held together in the law given to them and believe in the Creator, just as they had received, and not have a starting point to fall away into the polytheism of the nations. We will present the necessary thing in this way. 'The nations,' as it is written also in the law of the Jews, 'will hear of divinations and omens'; but to that people it is said: 'But to you the Lord your God has not given thus.' And it is added to this: 'The Lord your God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers.' If, then, the nations use divinations, either through 'divinations' or through birds or through entrails or through belly-talkers or through those who promise sacrifices or through Chaldeans who calculate births, all of which were forbidden to the Jews. If the Jews had no consolation of knowledge of things to come, they would have been led by the same human curiosity about knowledge of future things, and they would have despised their own as having nothing divine in themselves, and they would not have accepted a prophet after Moses, nor would they have written down their words, but they would have become deserters to the divinations and oracles of the nations, or they would have tried to establish something of this kind among themselves. So it is not absurd that the prophets among them spoke beforehand as a consolation to those who long for such things, so that even Samuel prophesied about donkeys that had been lost, and the one written in the third book of Kings prophesied about the illness of the king's child. How would the Jewish elders, who preside over the law, have rebuked the one who wants to take divination from idols? Just as Elijah is found rebuking Ochozias, saying: 'If, because there is no God in Israel, you go to seek in Baal the fly god of Accaron'

bible_refs.note: The Lord your God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers

pass_b_english: Since we have now come to the discourse about the prophets, what follows will not be useless for the Jews, who believe they spoke by the divine Spirit, but also for the fair-minded among the Greeks. To them we shall say that it is necessary to accept that the Jews also had prophets, if indeed they were to hold together in the law given them and believe in the Creator, just as they had received it, and so as not to have a starting point to fall away into the polytheism of the nations. We shall demonstrate the necessity thus: 'The nations,' as it is written also in the law of the Jews, 'will hear of divinations and omens'; but to that people it was said: 'But to you the Lord your God has not given thus.' And this is added to it: 'The Lord your God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers' (Deuteronomy 18:15). If, then, the nations use divinations—whether through 'divinations' or through birds or through entrails or through ventriloquists or through those who promise sacrifices or through Chaldeans calculating births—all of which were forbidden to the Jews. If the Jews had no consolation of knowledge of things to come, they would have been led by that same human curiosity about knowledge of the future, and they would have despised their own as having nothing divine in themselves, and they would not have accepted a prophet after Moses, nor would they have written down their words, but they would have become deserters to the divinations and oracles of the nations, or they would have tried to establish something of this kind among themselves. So it is not absurd that the prophets among them spoke beforehand as a consolation to those who long for such things, so that even Samuel prophesied about lost donkeys, and the one recorded in the third book of Kings prophesied about the illness of a royal child (1 Kings 21:26). How would the Jewish elders, who preside over the law, have rebuked the one who wants to obtain divination from idols? Just as Elijah is found rebuking Ochozias, saying: 'If, because there is no God in Israel, you go to seek in Baal the fly god of Accaron.'
